title: Paper clay pierced lantern globe
subtitle: A spherical lantern with pierced starfield pattern for a tea light
excerpt: A hollow sphere of air-dry paper clay about 14 cm in diameter sits over a tea light and casts a dotted starfield pattern onto the wall behind it. The sphere is built from two pinch-pot halves joined at the equator, then pierced all over with a needle tool before drying. No kiln is needed: paper clay air-dry sets at room temperature.
sourceNotes: Technique derived from first principles. Sphere-from-two-halves construction referenced from general hand-building practice. V&A open-access collection for historical pierced lantern form reference.

content.text: A globe lantern in
paper clay

is a hollow sphere about 14 cm in diameter, pierced with hundreds of tiny holes that let tea-light glow scatter across a wall as a point-light pattern. The cellulose fibres in paper clay make it strong enough to build thinly and resist the stress of piercing without crumbling. No kiln is needed: the sphere sets at room temperature in two to four days. Place over a flameless LED tea light for safety.

materials.name: Clay slip (paper clay thinned with water)
PVA glue diluted 50/50 with water (for sealing)

content.text: Preparation

Paper clay air-dry is sold in packages like standard air-dry clay. It feels slightly stiffer out of the package. Warm a piece by kneading it in your palms for two to three minutes before shaping. The paper fibres make it harder to pinch than plain air-dry clay initially, but the added strength means you can build walls down to 5 mm without the sphere collapsing. Work on a canvas sheet. Keep unused clay sealed tightly.
Forming the two halves
Divide the clay into two equal portions, roughly 190 g each. Roll each into a smooth ball. Form the first
pinch pot
: press your thumb into the centre of the ball to about halfway through. Pinch between thumb and forefinger, rotating the ball a quarter-turn after each pinch. Work from the base upward.

Aim for a hemispherical bowl shape with walls 5-6 mm thick and an opening diameter of 14 cm at the rim. The base of the hemisphere should be slightly thicker (7-8 mm) to give strength at the joining line.
Smooth the interior of the hemisphere with a damp sponge and the exterior with a wooden rib. Set aside and cover with a cloth.
Repeat for the second half. Both halves should match in rim diameter and wall height. Set them rim to rim to check they align.
Joining the sphere
Allow both halves to stiffen for 30 to 45 minutes until they hold their shape without sagging. They should be soft but no longer floppy. Use the
score-and-slip
method: score the rim of each half with a needle tool and apply slip to both scored faces.

Press the two halves together with the rims aligned. Rotate one half slightly against the other to seat the slip join. Hold firm for 30 seconds, then set the sphere upright on a wadded cloth ring to stop it rolling.
Blend the exterior equator seam with a wooden rib, pressing clay from each side over the join line. Smooth with a damp sponge to create a continuous surface.

Cut a 4 cm hole in the base of the sphere using a fettling knife. This hole allows the LED tea light to be placed inside and provides the airflow that any real candle would need. The LED tea light fits through this opening.
Piercing the starfield pattern
Wait until the sphere has reached a firm
leather-hard

state before piercing. Piercing into too-soft clay closes the holes as the clay springs back; piercing into too-dry clay crumbles the edges of each hole. Leather-hard clay cuts cleanly and holds the hole open.

Hold the sphere in one hand (or rest it in a cloth ring) and press the needle tool straight through the wall with a firm, steady push. Do not twist: push in and withdraw in the same line. Each hole should pass cleanly through the 5-6 mm wall.

For a random starfield: pierce holes at varying intervals across the entire sphere surface, spacing them roughly 8-15 mm apart. Cluster more holes at the upper half where the light effect will be most visible.
For a constellation pattern: mark constellation shapes with a pencil on the surface first, then pierce along the lines. Leave at least 8 mm between adjacent holes to prevent the wall weakening.
Vary the needle tool diameter if available: a thicker hole gives a larger light spot; a finer hole gives a pinprick. A mix of sizes gives depth to the starfield effect.
After piercing, smooth the exterior surface gently with a barely damp sponge to remove any raised clay burrs around the holes. Do not press too hard or you will close the smaller holes.
Drying
Allow the sphere to air-dry to
bone-dry

over two to four days at room temperature. Rest it on a cloth ring to keep the base hole clear and allow air to circulate inside the sphere as well as outside. Cover loosely with a cloth for the first day to slow the exterior surface drying relative to the interior. Paper clay tolerates drying better than standard air-dry clay, but a sphere has no flat face to rest on, so support matters throughout.
Sealing and finishing

Apply a coat of 50/50 PVA and water to the exterior of the bone-dry sphere. Use a soft brush and work the sealer into the area around each pierced hole. Allow to dry. Apply a second coat. The interior does not need sealing. For a metallic finish, brush the sealed exterior with bronze or copper acrylic. Keep the holes clear: do not seal directly over them.
Use and care

Use only with a flameless LED tea light. Paper clay air-dry is porous and will absorb moisture from a real candle flame, and is not tested for proximity to naked flames. Keep the lantern on a flat stable surface. The sphere is decorative only; handle with care as the pierced walls are thinner than an unpierced vessel. Dust with a soft brush.
Variations
Make a flattened oval form rather than a sphere by pressing both halves slightly before joining, giving an egg shape that sits more stably without a cloth ring.
Pierce a single word or initial in large dot-matrix letters across the sphere face, spacing dots 5 mm apart, for a personalised lantern.
Make two smaller globes at 9 cm diameter and place them as a pair flanking a central larger globe for a grouped display.
Troubleshooter

items.problem: Sphere loses its round shape during drying
items.cause: One half was softer than the other when joined, causing the sphere to sag
items.fix: Rest the sphere in a cloth ring throughout drying to support its shape. Rotate 180 degrees each day so no single point bears all the weight

items.cause: The clay was too soft; the walls sprang back after the needle was withdrawn
items.fix: Wait until leather-hard. Test on a concealed area of the sphere first: a clean hole that stays open is the correct stage

items.problem: Equator seam cracks open during drying
items.cause: The two halves were at different moisture levels when joined, so they shrink at different rates
items.fix: At leather-hard, press fresh paper clay slip into the crack and smooth. Allow to dry slowly

items.problem: Walls crack in a web pattern across multiple holes
items.cause: Holes were placed too close together, leaving insufficient clay between them
items.fix: Keep at least 8 mm between adjacent holes. If cracking occurs, press paper clay slip into the cracks while still at leather-hard
